```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(drmTMB)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>")
```

Does survival vary with temperature anomaly? The six deliberately separated observations below illustrate an estimation problem: all survivors have positive anomalies and all failures have negative anomalies. They are invented teaching data, not biological evidence. A binomial coefficient can run toward infinity under this separation. Independent normal priors can keep selected coefficients finite. Choose their scales in the units of your predictors and the link-scale effect you consider plausible. The fit is a penalized or maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) point estimate; this workflow does not sample a full posterior. The prior table shown below can also target Gaussian residual SDs, supported random-intercept SDs, and correlations.

```{r separation}
d <- data.frame(x=c(-3,-2,-1,1,2,3), y=c(0,0,0,1,1,1))
p <- drm_priors(
  drm_prior_normal("mu", "(Intercept)", mean=0, sd=3),
  drm_prior_normal("mu", "x", mean=0, sd=2)
)
drm_resolve_priors(bf(mu=y~x), binomial(), d, p)
f <- drmTMB(bf(mu=y~x), binomial(), data=d, priors=p)
coef(f, dpar="mu")
```

Let `x` be temperature anomaly in degrees Celsius and `y` survival (0 or 1). In this example, a one-degree warmer anomaly multiplies fitted survival odds by `r round(exp(coef(f, dpar="mu")[["x"]]), 2)`, from a slope of `r round(coef(f, dpar="mu")[["x"]], 2)` log-odds units. These values depend on the chosen priors. Here `mu` is the event-probability parameter and its predictor uses the logit link. The priors act on the intercept and slope of that predictor. A proper prior on only one coefficient cannot guarantee a finite estimate for every unpenalized direction. Both directions receive priors in this example.

For a simulated growth-rate response, suppose temperature anomaly predicts both mean growth and variation among observations. For Gaussian data, `mu` describes location and `sigma` residual scale. The `mu` predictor is on the response scale, while the `sigma` predictor is on log SD. The two blocks can receive different priors even when both contain a column named `x`.

```{r gaussian}
set.seed(5105)
g <- data.frame(x=rnorm(120))
g$y <- 0.4 + 1.2*g$x + rnorm(120, sd=exp(-0.3 + 0.2*g$x))
gp <- drm_priors(
  drm_prior_normal("mu", "x", sd=2),
  drm_prior_normal("sigma", "x", sd=0.5)
)
drm_resolve_priors(bf(mu=y~x, sigma=~x), gaussian(), g, gp)
gf <- drmTMB(bf(mu=y~x, sigma=~x), data=g, priors=gp)
coef(gf)
```

In this simulated example, the fitted mean changes by `r round(coef(gf, dpar="mu")[["x"]], 2)` response units per degree. The residual SD is multiplied by `r round(exp(coef(gf, dpar="sigma")[["x"]]), 2)` per degree, from a log-SD slope of `r round(coef(gf, dpar="sigma")[["x"]], 2)`. These fitted associations describe the teaching data.

## Repeated observations within groups

If observations share a group, a Gaussian model can include one independent
random intercept in the mean. These invented growth observations have three
measurements per group. The prior still acts on the fixed temperature slope;
the group SD is estimated without a prior.

```{r gaussian-group}
re <- data.frame(x=rep(c(-1, 0, 1), 6), group=factor(rep(1:6, each=3)))
re$y <- 0.5 + 0.6*re$x + rep(c(-0.5, 0.2, 0.7, -0.3, 0.4, -0.4), each=3) +
  rep(c(0.1, -0.2, 0.1), 6)
rp <- drm_priors(drm_prior_normal("mu", "x", mean=0.2, sd=0.8))
rf <- drmTMB(bf(mu=y~x + (1 | group), sigma=~1), data=re, priors=rp)
coef(rf, dpar="mu")
logLik(rf)
```

The fit integrates over the group intercepts and adds the coefficient prior
once to the marginal negative log-likelihood. `logLik(rf)` is the data
log-likelihood at the resulting penalized estimates, without the prior term.

## Use one table for coefficients, SDs, and correlations

The prior table gives each row a distribution and target class. Normal and
Student-t rows apply to named regression coefficients on their predictor link
scale. Gamma rows target a residual SD or a supported random-intercept SD on
its natural SD scale. The table writes Gamma parameters as `gamma(mean,shape)`;
the density is normalized and receives no log-SD Jacobian when the optimizer
uses log SD. An LKJ row targets a residual or random-slope correlation. The
resolved preview identifies each target before fitting.

```{r prior-table}
set.seed(5107)
tabdat <- expand.grid(group=seq_len(24), x=seq(-1, 1, length.out=8))
tabdat$group <- factor(tabdat$group)
ngroup <- length(levels(tabdat$group))
tabdat$y <- 0.3 + 0.7*tabdat$x +
  rnorm(ngroup, sd=0.45)[tabdat$group] +
  rnorm(nrow(tabdat), sd=exp(-0.2 + 0.15*tabdat$x))
f <- bf(mu=y ~ x + (1 | group), sigma=~1)
prior_table <- data.frame(
  prior=c("normal(0,2)", "student_t(0,1,4)", "gamma(0.55,2)",
          "gamma(0.6,2)"),
  class=c("fixef", "fixef", "residual_sd", "ranef_sd"),
  dpar=c("mu", "mu", "sigma", "mu"),
  coef=c("(Intercept)", "x", "(Intercept)", "group"),
  scale=c("link", "link", "natural_sd", "natural_sd")
)
drm_resolve_priors(f, gaussian(), tabdat, prior_table)
tf <- drmTMB(f, data=tabdat, priors=prior_table)
c(logLik=as.numeric(logLik(tf)), log_prior=tf$log_prior,
  data_plus_log_prior=as.numeric(logLik(tf)) + tf$log_prior,
  penalized_nll=tf$penalized_objective)
```

Here the table regularizes the mean slope, the residual SD, and the independent
random-intercept SD for `group`. These are separate targets in one Gaussian
model. `logLik(tf)` remains the unpenalized data likelihood at the penalized
estimate, and `tf$log_prior` supplies the prior contribution. Their sum is the
maximized penalized criterion; `tf$penalized_objective` stores its negative,
which is the quantity minimized by the optimizer.

An LKJ prior can instead target the correlation in a random intercept-slope
block. The current Gamma random-effect SD rows support independent random
intercepts; do not combine one with a correlated random-slope block. The
correlation row uses the exact grouping factor and coefficient pair:

```{r slope-correlation}
cor_dat <- expand.grid(group=seq_len(24), x=seq(-1, 1, length.out=8))
cor_dat$group <- factor(cor_dat$group)
ng <- nlevels(cor_dat$group)
u0 <- rnorm(ng, sd=0.45)
u1 <- 0.25*u0 + rnorm(ng, sd=0.18)
cor_dat$y <- 0.3 + 0.7*cor_dat$x + u0[cor_dat$group] +
  u1[cor_dat$group]*cor_dat$x + rnorm(nrow(cor_dat), sd=0.3)
f_cor <- bf(mu=y ~ x + (1 + x | group), sigma=~1)
cor_prior_table <- data.frame(
  prior=c("normal(0,2)", "lkj(2)"),
  class=c("fixef", "correlation"),
  dpar=c("mu", "mu"),
  coef=c("x", ""),
  group=c("", "group"),
  from_coef=c("", "(Intercept)"),
  to_coef=c("", "x"),
  scale=c("link", "natural_correlation")
)
drm_resolve_priors(f_cor, gaussian(), cor_dat, cor_prior_table)
cor_fit <- drmTMB(f_cor, data=cor_dat, priors=cor_prior_table)
c(data_logLik=as.numeric(logLik(cor_fit)),
  log_prior=cor_fit$log_prior,
  data_plus_log_prior=as.numeric(logLik(cor_fit)) + cor_fit$log_prior,
  penalized_nll=cor_fit$penalized_objective)
```

The table is explicit about the parameters each row targets. A correlation
prior does not add an SD prior to either random-effect coefficient. Gamma
priors on individual SDs in a correlated random-slope block are not currently
supported.

For two Gaussian responses, a separate `rho12` row can regularize their
residual correlation. This route permits exactly one LKJ prior on `rho12`,
optionally combined with Normal or Student-t rows for exact `mu1` and `mu2`
coefficients. You may write `sigma1 = ~1` and `sigma2 = ~1` explicitly; use
intercept-only scale formulas for this prior route:

```{r bivariate-correlation}
bivdat <- data.frame(x=seq(-1, 1, length.out=40))
err <- matrix(rnorm(2*nrow(bivdat)), ncol=2) %*%
  chol(matrix(c(1, 0.45, 0.45, 1), nrow=2))
bivdat$y1 <- 0.2 + 0.5*bivdat$x + err[, 1]
bivdat$y2 <- -0.1 - 0.3*bivdat$x + err[, 2]
biv_formula <- bf(mu1=y1 ~ x, mu2=y2 ~ x)
biv_prior_table <- data.frame(
  prior=c("normal(0,2)", "lkj(2)"),
  class=c("fixef", "correlation"),
  dpar=c("mu1", "rho12"),
  coef=c("x", "(Intercept)"),
  scale=c("link", "natural_correlation")
)
drm_resolve_priors(biv_formula, biv_gaussian(), bivdat, biv_prior_table)
biv_fit <- drmTMB(biv_formula, family=biv_gaussian(), data=bivdat,
                  priors=biv_prior_table)
c(data_logLik=as.numeric(logLik(biv_fit)),
  log_prior=biv_fit$log_prior,
  data_plus_log_prior=as.numeric(logLik(biv_fit)) + biv_fit$log_prior)
```

With a varying residual SD, the marginal objective can have several local minima. A convergence flag does not show that the lowest minimum was found. Compare fits from multiple starts, for example with `control = drm_control(se = FALSE, logsigma_clamp = NULL, multi_start = 5)`. In the independent validation grid, the default start reached an inferior boundary minimum in one fixture; this multiple-start configuration passed all twelve fixtures. Multiple starts do not guarantee a global optimum.

To penalize a whole coefficient block, choose the intercept policy explicitly. The ridge constructor adds `0.5 * lambda * sum(beta^2)` to the negative data log-likelihood. For positive lambda, it has the same optimum and curvature as a mean-zero normal prior with SD `1/sqrt(lambda)`; the ridge objective omits the normal density constant.

```{r ridge}
r <- drm_priors(drm_prior_ridge("mu", "all", lambda=0.25,
                               intercept="exclude"))
drm_resolve_priors(bf(mu=y~x), gaussian(), g, r)
```

Exact coefficient names refer to the final design matrix, including factor contrasts and interactions. `coef="all"` includes or excludes the conventional intercept using design metadata. Level columns in a no-intercept factor formula remain ordinary coefficients. No automatic centring or scaling occurs. To discover factor and interaction names before selecting a column, inspect `colnames(model.matrix(~ f*x, data))`, using the predictor formula for that distributional parameter; then check `drm_resolve_priors()` on the complete-case data you will fit. Unknown names, empty or overlapping selections and rank-deficient designs fail before fitting. Zero lambda adds nothing but still validates the requested selection and design.

For the table fit, `logLik(tf)` reports the data log-likelihood at the
penalized estimate. The fit stores `tf$log_prior` and separate penalty fields.
`summary()` and `vcov()` describe local penalized-Hessian curvature, not
calibrated uncertainty. Confidence intervals and profile comparisons are not
available for active priors. AIC, BIC, and AICc return warning-labelled
diagnostics using the unpenalized data likelihood and nominal parameter count;
ordinary model comparisons require unpenalized refits. Likelihood-ratio tests
warn and refuse prior fits. Point predictions and simulations use the fitted
parameter values, without drawing coefficient uncertainty. These penalized
fits have not been validated for `tmbstan` posterior sampling.

The univariate coefficient-prior route accepts complete, unit-weight Gaussian
identity and binomial-logit models with dense, unaggregated fixed-effect
designs. Gaussian mean formulas may include one or two unlabelled independent
random intercepts with distinct grouping partitions. Gamma random-effect SD
priors currently target these independent mean random intercepts. They do not
target an SD inside a correlated random-slope block. A separate LKJ row can
target the correlation in a two-coefficient Gaussian random-intercept-slope
block. Bivariate Gaussian models have a narrower route: exactly one LKJ prior
on residual `rho12`, optionally combined with Normal or Student-t priors on
exact `mu1` or `mu2` coefficients. Normal priors on mean and log residual-SD
coefficients also support one phylogenetic mean intercept with a matching
phylogenetic SD-regression formula in complete-data Gaussian ML models with
full-rank fixed-effect designs; they do not regularize the phylogenetic
SD-regression coefficients. The existing phylogenetic SD penalty is distinct
from the coefficient and Gamma SD table rows. Random-slope SD priors, scale
random effects, weights, REML, MSPL, other response families, and unsupported
structured combinations are refused. Fits with active priors use an unclamped
log-scale predictor; when passing `drm_control()`, set `logsigma_clamp=NULL`
explicitly, then use the resolved preview to confirm every target before
fitting. A wider prior or a
different coding can change the result, so compare several scientifically
plausible scales.

With `engine = "julia"`, Gaussian mean formulas with ordinary random effects
currently refuse factor predictors; the native TMB route supports them.
